title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: Price increase (6%) without promotion
drivers.evidence: Recent week at $4.08 saw only 3 units (x0.29 vs baseline); past promotions show noise-adjusted uplift of x1.45, but this is a non-promotional price hike, so effect is negative.

drivers.name: Supplier delivery short
drivers.evidence: Planner note warns of short delivery; this introduces supply risk, likely reducing sell-through even if demand is present.

adjustment.analysis: The target week has no events, but a 6% price increase to $4.08 (vs. $3.85 regular). Past promotions show a median uplift of x2.15, but noise-adjusted to x1.45. However, this price increase is not a promotion, and the recent week (2026-10-05) at $4.08 saw only 3 units (x0.29 vs baseline), indicating price sensitivity. The planner note of a short delivery suggests supply risk, which may suppress demand. No past Thanksgiving week (before event) showed a meaningful lift (noise-adjusted x1.0). The classical model's x1.0 is a starting point, but supply risk and recent high-price failure justify a downward adjustment. Evidence is thin but consistent on price sensitivity and supply concern.

  events: none
  shelf price: 4.08 (+6.0% vs regular price 3.85)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.2 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 25.3 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 19.6

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-85% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
